caption:
Nvidia told server makers to stop shipping its AI servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reports.
New US rules give cloud providers in the region 90 days to get export licenses, and no one is sure how.

Should chip makers police who rents their servers?

site_article.seo_title: Nvidia halts AI server shipments to Southeast Asia, FT says
site_article.seo_description: Nvidia paused AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia after new US rules gave cloud providers 90 days to get export licenses.
site_article.answer_summary: Nvidia asked server makers such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping its AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries while it works out how to comply with new US export rules aimed at Chinese access to rented computing power.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia has told the companies that build its servers to stop shipping systems with its AI chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported on November 26, 2026, citing three people familiar with the matter. The report was carried by The National and the Malaysian tech site Lowyat.NET.

According to the report, server makers including Dell and Supermicro have informed customers in the four countries that Nvidia will not authorize their pending orders to be shipped. It is not clear whether the pause is temporary or how long it could last. The sources said Nvidia and its manufacturing partners are trying to work out how to comply with the latest United States export rules.
Nvidia declined to comment on the suspension, Lowyat.NET reported, and Dell and Supermicro did not respond to the Financial Times.

Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia have become popular destinations for Chinese AI developers looking for Nvidia's most advanced processors, which Washington bars from direct export to China, both outlets said. One common route has been to rent computing power from cloud providers outside mainland China, which buy servers built around Nvidia chips and lease out the capacity.

The shipment halt follows new rules introduced by the US Commerce Department the previous week to close that route. Under the rules, regional cloud providers must obtain export licenses within 90 days and show that none of their end users are restricted entities, Lowyat.NET reported. A cloud provider executive in the region told the Financial Times that companies do not know how to apply for the license before the deadline and that the new rule came without guidance on how to carry it out.
What is at stake for Nvidia

Southeast Asia's growing data center industry has become an important source of revenue for Nvidia. Company accounts cited by the Financial Times show Nvidia booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, up 72 percent from a year earlier, according to The National. Nvidia also records some revenue from Taiwan and China through that unit, so the figure is not all regional sales.
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has argued in the past that allowing the company to sell chips in China would keep the country dependent on American technology, The National noted.

The halt shows how far the latest controls reach beyond China itself. By targeting rented computing power, Washington has made ordinary server orders in neighboring countries a compliance risk, and Nvidia appears to be pausing first and sorting out the paperwork later. For data center builders in the region, a 90 day licensing clock with no clear process means projects can stall even when the end customer has nothing to do with China.
Watch whether the Commerce Department publishes guidance on the new cloud licenses before the 90 day window closes, and whether Nvidia resumes shipments to customers who can show they qualify.
